item.title: Ancient wildfire study offers warning for a warming world
item.description: New research from the University of Aberdeen has revealed that periods of global warming can trigger long-lasting increases in wildfire activity, with ecosystems taking far longer to recover than previously thought. The study, recently published in Scientific Reports, provides the first detailed evidence of how wildfires responded to a major natural warming event around 65 million years ago, the Danian hyperthermal. This work offers important insights into the risks facing today's world as climate change drives more frequent and severe fires. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Suicidio en Argentina: ¿por qué es la principal causa de muerte violenta entre los jóvenes?
item.description: En Argentina, el aumento de los suicidios, especialmente entre los jóvenes, enciende las alertas sobre la salud mental. Entre las personas de 25 a 34 años, el suicidio se ha convertido en la principal causa de muerte, por delante de los accidentes de tráfico. ¿Qué hay detrás de esta realidad y cómo identificar las señales de alerta para prevenirla? Para profundizar en estas preguntas, conversamos con el doctor Demian Rodante, médico psiquiatra y psicoterapeuta especializado en salud mental. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Bank credit remains scarce in Bangladesh where climate risks are highest
item.description: For 34-year-old Saiful Gazi — a resident of Ramjannagar Union in Shyamnagar, Satkhira, an area highly vulnerable to climate change — securing institutional financing is a major struggle. Gazi, who supports a family of four, endured the devastating Cyclone Aila on May 25, 2009. Cyclone Aila claimed 190 lives and affected approximately 3.9 million people […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds
item.description: Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study. The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.
